speechtext: Expliquez.

subtopic: MEASURE REQUIRING REGISTRATION WITH CLERK OF PARLIAMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to require registration with the Clerk of Parliaments of all lobbyists; persons employed by others in an attempt to influence the public's elected representatives for or against enactment of laws. It would in no way interfere with lobbying or the right of
citizens to express their wishes to members of parliament, but as is done in several of the United States now, it would require the identification to the public of the private interests and motives of paid lobbyists.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to announce a change in the business of the house, which occurred as a result of discussions this morning. In view of the fact that we did not complete the debate on second reading of the Criminal Code last night, we agreed this morning that it would be desirable to change the order so that the debate on second reading might be resumed today in the hope that perhaps a decision will be taken before the close of this day. If that decision is taken we will then call the bill amending the Financial Administration Act for consideration during the balance of today.
The timetable in respect of the proposed government organization act will therefore be set back one day. We will commence the debate on that tomorrow. If it is not completed through the appropriate stages by tomorrow night, we will continue with that debate on Friday.
There were also discussions as to the manner of debating the government organization act. Perhaps I might take advantage at this time to put the suggestions on record. There might be general agreement on a relatively short discussion at the second reading stage, with possibly only one speaker from each party. Instead of lengthy and varied discussion on the first clause in the committee of the whole it might be agreeable that we deal with each part of the bill as an integral unit before proceeding to the next one. In this way we hope that the chairman of the committee might be more lenient in permitting a more general debate on the clauses at the beginning of each part, in respect of each department, than would normally be the case. It would seem possible in this way to deal with this in a more systematic and structured fashion.

POSSIBLE ABUSES OF DIPLOMATIC PRIVILEGES BY CANADIANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, is the Solicitor General able to answer the question I asked on Monday?

subtopic: POSSIBLE ABUSES OF DIPLOMATIC PRIVILEGES BY CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker on Monday last, as appears at page 5847 of Hansard, the hon. member asked me the following question:
In view of assertions made publicly by Mr. Paul Akehurst of Canadian Contemporary News concerning depositions in a civil case in California indicating possible abuses of diplomatic privileges by Canadians abroad, including a possible connection with narcotics offences in Mexico, will the minister consider making a statement to the house tomorrow on this serious issue?
I replied that I would be very glad to obtain the necessary information and bring forward a reply either Tuesday or Wednesday, depending on how quickly I could get the information.
I have examined this matter carefully. The facts are that the husband of the person involved in the civil case now before courts in California is a public servant who had been posted abroad prior to 1951, but who has not been posted abroad since that time. Nothing in the files involved him in any questionable activity and there were no abuses of diplomatic privileges by him. Allegations of abuse of diplomatic privilege were brought to the government's attention many years ago and were investigated at that time, but no evidence was found to support them. Those allegations only indirectly concerned him and did not directly or indirectly involve anyone else in the Canadian diplomatic service.
The allegations concerning narcotics offences involving the party to the California litigation were investigated at the time they were made, and no basis for criminal action was discovered. The investigation did indicate that the person concerned was under the care

of a physician, and drugs that were not narcotic drugs were being prescribed for the medical condition.
Although the question by the hon. member for Fundy-Royal did not ask about other investigations, I think 1 should add that there have been investigations relating to a bankruptcy in November 1966. This last mentioned matter is still current.
As to the civil proceedings now before the courts in California, I am sure the house would not wish me to make any comment.

speechtext:
The other day, February 19, the hon. member for Egmont asked me a question which I promised to answer. He is more diligent than the hon. member for Greenwood in
February 26, 1969

Inquiries of the Ministry following up his questions, so I will answer his question first.
The hon. member for Egmont asked me whether I would investigate a recent report. I quote the hon. member's words:
All male Blafran refugees in Port Harcourt are in danger of being executed?
The report originated in a Radio Biafra broadcast of February 17 which alleged that all able bodied men in a certain refugee camp had been transferred to Port Harcourt for execution and that 120 men were executed during the week beginning February 10 at Port Harcourt.
First I would note that the Lagos government denied these reports on February 18. Second, General Hamilton, the Canadian representative on the Observer Team which visited Port Harcourt February 18 to 20 inclusive has informed me that the team visited the federal prison in Port Harcourt, and two refugee centres, the latter housing 3,000 and 4,000 refugees respectively. There was no evidence to support an allegation that all male Biafran refugees in Port Harcourt are in danger of being executed. Refugee camps appear to be well administered and are receiving medical aid and food from the Nigerian Red Cross and the International Red Cross. Many male refugees were seen and ample opportunity was afforded to them to voice their complaints or fears. None was offered. The team spoke to many civilians, including the head of the I.C.R.C. there. If 120 male refugees had been slain rumours would certainly have reached them.
